sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content: Global equities rallied broadly in a risk-on week as a surprise US jobs contraction lowered rate-hike fears and Strait of Hormuz reopening hopes eased oil. MSCI World rose roughly **+2.5%** (approx., verify before merging), MSCI Developed Markets a similar **+2.5%** (approx., verify before merging) and MSCI Emerging Markets about **+1%** (approx., verify before merging). The S&P 500 jumped **3.6%** to a record **7,757.64**, its best week since April, while the MAG7 mega-cap tech cohort led the advance on renewed AI enthusiasm, lifting the Nasdaq **5.2%**. Europe's Euro Stoxx 50 gained **2.4%** to about **6,523.86**; Japan's Nikkei 225 climbed **2.78%** to **65,606.71**, China's CSI 300 added roughly **0.9%** (approx., verify before merging) and Hong Kong's Hang Seng finished firmer.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
US equities advanced strongly, with several indices notching fresh records. The S&P 500 rose **3.6%** to a record **7,757.64**, the Nasdaq Composite climbed **5.2%** to **26,690.62** and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added **3.0%**, all posting their best weekly gains since April as favourable earnings and renewed AI enthusiasm powered technology and communication-services leadership.

The pivotal catalyst was a soft July payrolls report, which showed employers unexpectedly shed **23,000** jobs against forecasts near **+80,000**, with May and June revised lower by a combined **103,000** and the slowest wage growth in nearly five years. Markets read the weakness as bad news being good news, easing inflation angst.

With the Fed's target range held at **3.50%-3.75%**, futures pared tightening bets and now assign less than a **50%** probability to a September hike. Optimism over a potential US-Iran deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz further buoyed sentiment into the weekend.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equities extended their advance, with the pan-European STOXX Europe 600 rising **1.70%** in local-currency terms to a fourth consecutive record close and its best week since June.

Regional bourses were firmly higher: Germany's DAX gained **2.69%**, Italy's FTSE MIB **2.96%** and France's CAC 40 **2.41%**, while the Euro Stoxx 50 added **2.4%** to close near **6,523.86**. Technology heavyweights such as ASML and SAP led, tracking Wall Street's exuberance, with resilient earnings and firmer risk appetite underpinning cyclicals.

The geopolitical backdrop stayed volatile, but hopes of a Strait of Hormuz reopening and softer oil supported sentiment. Falling global yields after the weak US jobs print and a benign rate outlook helped keep European risk assets bid through the close.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asian markets were mostly firmer, led by a volatile but strong week in Japan. The Nikkei 225 gained **2.78%** to **65,606.71**, surging **3.66%** to **66,300.44** on Wednesday before giving back part of the move, as heavyweight chip and AI-linked shares oscillated.

Currency dynamics again shaped the tape after recent coordinated US-Japanese intervention: the yen retained much of its intervention-driven strength, and a weak 10-year auction lifted JGB yields, complicating the export-heavy equity backdrop even as shares rallied.

Chinese equities firmed, with the mainland CSI 300 rising roughly **0.9%** (approx., verify before merging) and Hong Kong's Hang Seng closing higher, though mid-week chip jitters tempered gains. Easing Middle East tension and Hormuz reopening optimism supported sentiment across Asia ex-Japan.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The US dollar softened as the surprise July payrolls contraction pared Fed tightening expectations and narrowed rate differentials, leaving the greenback on the back foot across much of the G10.

Sterling was resilient but rangebound, with GBP/USD broadly flat on the week and still trapped in the **1.32-1.35** band that has defined 2026; with domestic fundamentals gaining little FX traction, the pound remained beholden to the dollar, risk sentiment and energy prices. The euro pulled back modestly from a seven-week peak despite the softer dollar backdrop.

The yen stayed a focal point: Japan's larger intervention footprint kept it supported and made investors think twice about JPY-funded carry trades, reinforcing two-way risk in USD/JPY.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Oil dominated the commodity complex amid intense headline risk around the Strait of Hormuz. Brent tumbled **5.3%** on Tuesday to around **$79** a barrel, its lowest since mid-July, on optimism over an Iran-Oman shipping corridor, before rebounding above **$83** as a durable agreement failed to materialise; Brent ended near **$83.46** and WTI around **$78.05**.

Gold advanced, rising about **1.4%** to roughly **$4,135** an ounce, supported by falling real yields after the soft US jobs data and its dual role as inflation hedge and safe haven as Middle East tensions ebbed and flowed.

The net easing in energy prices and geopolitical risk fed directly into the week's risk-on tone, pulling bond yields lower and supporting a firmer bid across credit.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
Sovereign yields fell as the weak July payrolls report reset the rates outlook. The 10-year UST eased to around **4.64%**, retreating from recent highs as traders scaled back expectations for further Fed tightening.

The Fed's target range was held at **3.50%-3.75%**, and markets now assign less than a **50%** probability to a September hike, with a majority of futures traders expecting policy to stay on hold; the slowest wage growth in nearly five years reinforced the dovish repricing.

Credit tone was firm: high-yield bonds outperformed Treasuries in the risk-on rally, aided by light primary supply, lower oil and optimism over a potential US-Iran deal. Investment-grade was steady, leaving the broader backdrop constructive but data-dependent.
